newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Astrid Lindgren remains amazed at Pippi's success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Astrid Lindgren remains amazed at Pippi's success.

text.p: Sweden's best known author, Astrid Lindgren, who turns 90 this year, remains amazed at the success of the characters she has created.
Generations of children across the world have grown up with the red haired, freckle-faced Pippi Longstocking, the mischievous Emil and Ronia the Robber's Daughter.
But Lindgren, whose fraility and failing eyesight now prevent her from writing, said she had never set out to entertain others, just to amuse herself and her two children.
"I wrote to amuse myself, nothing else," Lindgren told Reuters during an interview in her comfortable apartment overlooking a picturesque Stockholm park.
"I never thought in any way of the children who were going to read these books. But it seems that what I enjoy myself amuses all kinds of children."

Although Lindgren did not set out for a literary career, there is no doubting her enjoyment of her work, with 30 books and several plays to her name, many of which have been made into films, television series, radio shows and cartoons.
Lindgren moved to Stockholm from her family's farm in Smaland in southern Sweden when she was 19 and worked in offices, including a publishing house, while she brought up her children.
Her literary debut did not come until the age of 37 in 1944 when she won second prize in a contest with her book, "The Confidences of Britt-Mari".
PIPPI'S LAUNCH MADE LINDGREN'S SUCCESS
But her real success came a year later when she introduced the public to Pippi Longstocking, a wild little girl who appealed to the adventurous streak in most children.

"My daughter, Karin, was sick in bed and asked me to tell her about Pippi Longstocking. She had invented the name at that very moment but I didn't ask her who this Pippi was. I just started to tell her about a girl with such a funny name," said Lindgren, with the soft lilt of an experienced storyteller.
"From then on my daughter kept asking me to tell her everything about Pippi Longstocking.
"Shortly afterwards I broke my ankle and had to stay in bed for a few days so I decided to write down the stories about Pippi. I showed them to a publisher...and that was how it started."
Pippi revolutionised Swedish children's literature.
The fantastic stories were a sharp contrast from the usual conformist children's literature found in Sweden until then.
The independent little girl, who remains nine on paper but turned 50 in 1995, lives alone in a big house, can lift a horse with one hand and has a pet monkey.
"It was such a success that all the children in Sweden got the book as a Christmas present that year," said Lindgren.

Lindgren's books are still the most popular with Swedish children. A study of borrowings from libraries across the country found Pippi and Emil books topped the lending list, borrowed 1.6 million times in 1995 from a total of 105 million.
She has sold more than 100 million books in 55 languages and won a long list of Swedish and international awards.
In 1986 the much-loved author was named Swede of the Year.
LINDGREN SAYS STORIES HAVE NO HIDDEN MEARNING

Many of her stories include glimpses from her childhood in the country, with her books full of local sayings and tastes of a farm life -- and all with characters full of energy and spirit, like the author herself.
But Lindgren, a strident campaigner for animal rights, insists there was never meant to be a hidden agenda behind any of her stories.
"I haven't intended any meaning at all," she said.
When Lindgren has wanted to get a message across she has made sure it really hits home.
In 1976, after receiving a tax demand that outstripped her income, she wrote a satirical fairy tale in a Swedish newspaper, parodying Sweden's taxation system.

A lifelong supporter of Sweden's ruling Social Democrat party, Lindgren had always said she paid Sweden's high taxes gladly -- until a tax claim arrived asking for over 100 percent of her annual earnings.

Her story about a country where just such a tax rate existed struck a chord with many heavily-taxed Swedes. Fiscal policy became a major issue at the next election and the Social Democrats lost power.
"I was amazed the day the story appeared to have my whole room here full of flowers," said Lindgren, with a twinkle in her vivid, blue eyes.

"It was a completely crazy idea to have this tax law but the authorities had ignored everyone's complaints until I wrote that story. Doctors and lawyers and everyone said it had been impossible to get anything done about this until then.
"I think it all depends how you express yourself if you want to get a message across."
PASSION FOR ANIMAL RIGHTS
Lindgren's love of animals has fuelled her second passion in life after writing -- campaigning for animal rights and against battery farming in particular.
"I grew up on a farm where everybody treated the animals like people. They were our friends. I never thought that I later in life would have to be outraged by their suffering," she said.

Her strong character and immense charm won her a promise at her 80th birthday party from then prime minister Ingvar Carlsson that he would present a new animal rights laws over the treatment of battery hens.
But his promise never came to fruition.
"Nothing has happened yet and I really cannot do any more about it. I am too old now," said Lindgren with a tired sigh.
"If I was 10 years younger it would be a different story."
